Furthermore, by means of a two-laser repumping scheme, we show an enhanced photoluminescence and emission intensity which can be utilized to realize a new modality of far-field super-resolution imaging. Our findings expand current understanding of quantum emitters in hBN and show new potential ways of harnessing their nonlinear optical properties in sub-diffraction nanoscopy.

articleTitle: High-speed uni-travelling carrier photodiode at 1064nm wavelength
abstract: High-speed back-illuminated uni-traveling-carrier photodiodes (UTC PDs) at 1064nm are demonstrated grown on InP with 3-dB bandwidth of 16.8GHz, using InGaAsP as absorption layer. PDs with <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$40-\mu\mathrm{m}$</tex> -diameters deliver RF output power levels as high as 18.8 dBm at 14GHz. A model based on S-parameter fitting aimed at extracting parameter to assess the bandwidth limiting factors.

articleTitle: Analysis of emission characteristics of deep levels in GaN by direct photo excitation
abstract: Deep levels in GaN have been discussed so far, while phonon dynamics or thermal properties at point defects or complexes remain unclear. In most of articles, the photoluminescence analyses have been conducted using the excitation laser with greater photon energy than energy gap, while the carrier energy relaxation distorts the spectrum and intensity decay characteristics. In this report, we show the results of selective excitation of defect levels, which straightly reveals electronic transition properties in defects. A freestanding n-GaN grown by HVPE was measured by time resolved photoluminescence measurements using excitation wavelengths of 400, 363, 337 and 266 (nm). The former two corresponds to the below energy gap excitation. Red luminescence (RL) and green luminescence (GL) were investigated. As a result, the RL shows the high decay lifetime of 12 ns, while GL shows the longer lifetime than hundreds of ns. The energy of the upper level for RL is found to be located at a higher level than 3.1 eV from the valence band. The temperature dependence of the RL decay properties show that the radiative process is the main transition process, and that local phonon mode is confined in the vicinity of defects below 150 K.

articleTitle: Towards semiconductor-superconductor hybrid qubits based on InAs/Al core/shell nanowires
abstract: The transport properties of mesoscopic InAs nanowire and InAs/Al core/shell nanowire Josephson junctions are investigated. By using a normal conducting shunt resistor parallel to the junction, it is possible to extract the real supercurrent of the device due to the suppression of phase fluctuations. Additionally, we present both Shapiro and emission measurements for InAs and InAs/Al nanowires with different Te-doping levels. The occurrence of Shapiro steps at fractional voltage values indicate a strongly non-sinusoidal current phase-relation due to a high transparency of the semiconductor/superconductor interface,

articleTitle: Suppression of Three-Dimensional Pit Formation of InAs on GaSb(001) by Two-Step MBE
abstract: InAs heteroepitaxial growth on GaSb by molecular beam epitaxy was investigated. Pits tend to easily form on InAs surface at low temperature growth; however, they are suppressed by adding traces of Sb owing to its surfactant effect. We further investigated a method to eliminate pits without Sb irradiation for device applications. We found that as the growth temperature increased, size of the pits reduced. The pits were completely suppressed by applying a two-step low- and high-temperature InAs growth. Sb carryover from the underlying InAs was negligible and never contributed to the elimination of pits. Two factors seemed to be essential: (1) initial planar growth of InAs on GaSb favored at low temperature and (2) preference for a (001) plane rather than high-index crystal planes at high temperature.

articleTitle: Superconductor/Semiconductor Devices for Majorana Zero Modes
abstract: There is growing interest in material systems that both support Majorana zero modes (MZMs), relevant for quantum computing, and can be fabricated into complex and scalable geometries. So far, MZMs have been tentatively identified in individual InSb or InAs nanowires with induced superconductivity. Future tests of non-Abelian statistics will likely involve braiding or interferometric measurement, requiring branched or looped geometries, challenging to realize using individual nanowires.

articleTitle: Threshold and Resistive Switching Behaviors in Epitaxially Regrown GaN P-N Diodes for High Temperature Applications
abstract: Resistive random access memory (RRAM) has been extensively investigated due to its great potential in synaptic and neuromorphic computing applications. In the crossbar array of RRAM architecture, threshold switching selector devices are one of the crucial components to cut off the sneak current path of the unselected cells. In this paper, we report the first observation of threshold and resistive switching behaviors in epitaxially regrown vertical GaN p-n diodes. This mechanism was ascribed to the conductive path formed by traps in the insulating layer at the regrowth interface after soft breakdown. The device can reliably switch more than 1000 cycles at both room temperature and 300 °C with small fluctuation on the set and reset voltage. The set voltage increased with the increasing temperature due to the enhanced thermal detrapping effect that made it harder to form conductive path at high temperatures. The device showed memory behaviors when the reset voltage was higher than 4.4 V. These devices can be integrated with mature III-nitride high electron mobility transistors (HEMTs) technology and facilitate the development of GaN-based integrated circuits, especially for harsh environments such as high temperature and radiation environments.

articleTitle: Characterization of Nanowire Devices Using Nano-Focused X-Ray Beams
abstract: The long absorption length of hard X-rays makes them ideal tools for investigating electronic and optoelectronic devices in realistic operational conditions. Modern X-ray optics reach the relevant length scales for single nanoelectronic devices. Here, methods to investigate single nanowire devices with nanofocused X-rays are discussed. The X-rays are used both as pump and probe of semiconductor nanowire devices. Nanofocused X-ray diffraction was used to quantify bending and lattice tilt in strained core-shell nanowires as well as electrically biased nanowire devices. The carrier collection in single solar cell nanowires was probed with X-ray beam induced current. X-ray fluorescence mapping at 50 nm spatial resolution of Zn doping in solar cell nanowires revealed background doping and long gradients. The demonstrated methods are relevant for a wide range of nanoscale semiconductor devices.

articleTitle: High performance Fully-vertical GaN-on-Si power MOSFETs
abstract: We report the first demonstration of fully-vertical power MOSFETs on <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$6.6-\mu \mathrm{m}$</tex>-thick GaN grown on a 6-inch Si substrate by metal-organic chemical vapor deposition (MOCVD). A robust fabrication method was developed based on a selective and local removal of the Si substrate as well as the resistive GaN buffer layers, followed by a conformal deposition of a <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$35-\mu \mathrm{m}$</tex>-thick copper layer on the backside by electroplating, which provides excellent mechanical stability and electrical contact to the drain terminal. The fabrication process of the gate trench was optimized, improving considerably the effective mobility at the p-GaN channel and the output current of the devices. High performance fully-vertical GaN-on-Si MOSFETs are presented, with low specific on-resistance <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$(\mathrm{R}_{\mathrm{on},\mathrm{sp}})$</tex> of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$5\ \mathrm{m}\Omega \mathrm{cm}^{2}$</tex> and high off-state breakdown voltage (BV) of 520 V. Our results reveal a major step towards the realization of high performance GaN vertical power devices on cost-effective Si substrates.

articleTitle: Picosecond Time-Resolved Excitation Dynamics and Emission Manipulation of Eu3+ Ions Doped into GaN
abstract: In its trivalent form, Europium is well-known for its red emission at 620 nm; however, transitions at 590 nm and 545 nm are also possible if additional excited states are exploited. A systematic series of spectroscopy experiments were performed to understand the energy transfer and re-excitation processes in Eu doped GaN. The initial energy transfer from GaN to Eu<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3+</sup> was found to take place on a time scale of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$< 20\ \mathrm{ns}$</tex>. After the transfer, it was found that the <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">${}^{5}\mathrm{D}_{0}$</tex> state of Eu<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3+</sup> was populated with the highest probability. While still in the <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">${}^{5}\mathrm{D}_{0}$</tex> state, the Eu<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3+</sup> ion can be subsequently re-excited and end up in the <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">${}^{5}\mathrm{D}_{2},\ {}^{5}\mathrm{D}_{1}$</tex> or <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">${}^{5}\mathrm{D}_{0}$</tex> state. Temperature dependent results further elucidate the role <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">${}^{5}\mathrm{D}_{2}$</tex> state in these processes.

articleTitle: Molecular Beam Epitaxy of Transition Metal Nitrides for Superconducting Device Applications
abstract: Integration of epitaxial superconducting layers with semiconductor devices is expected to enable substantial performance benefits, design flexibility, and creation of novel device structures. Integration of superconducting transition metal nitrides (TMNs) with the wide bandgap group III-N semiconductors is especially appealing because of the close lattice match, similar crystal structures, and chemical and thermal compatibility of the TMN and III-N families of materials. We have previously reported on the use of a Scienta-Omicron PRO-75 RF-plasma molecular beam epitaxy (MBE) chamber equipped with an in-situ electron beam evaporator to epitaxially grow metallic niobium nitride (NbN<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">x</inf>) thin films and III-N/NbNx heterostructures on hexagonal SiC substrates. More recently, we have reported on growth of single-phase thin films of single-crystal hexagonal <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\gamma$</tex>-Ta<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf>N on 3-inch-diameter SiC substrates. In this presentation, we will discuss our recent work on the growth and superconducting properties of TMNs grown on SiC by MBE. The films were characterized in-situ using reflection high-energy electron diffraction, and ex-situ using optical and atomic-force microscopy, contactless sheet resistance, X-ray diffraction, cross-sectional transmission electron microscopy, and superconductivity measurements. We will discuss the MBE growth conditions for epitaxial superconducting NbNx and hexagonal <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\gamma$</tex>-Ta<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf>N on SiC.

articleTitle: Spectral Hole Burning Spectroscopy on Quantum Dashes and Quantum Dots for Dual-Frequency Laser Engineering
abstract: The homogeneous linewidth of two inhomogeneous media is investigated by Spectral Hole Burning in resonant excitation conditions for the purpose of dual-frequency VECSEL engineering. We performed Spectral Hole Burning experiments on InAs/InP Quantum Dashes and Quantum Dots, as well as on InGaAs/InP Quantum Wells to get a reference of homogeneous behavior. Experimental evidences show that Quantum Dots having different energies inside the whole QD population are less coupled than Quantum Dashes. At a low temperature of 77K, the homogeneous linewidth is only 0.73 meV for QDs versus 1.17 meV for QDashes. With increasing temperature, electronic coupling between the dots populates nanostructures at other energies than the excitation energy. However, a resonantly excited QD population remains visible up to 130 K, a larger temperature than for QDashes, and even at room temperature a signature of the excitation energy remains visible in the Spectral Hole Burning spectra.

articleTitle: Rectified Schottky diodes that use low-cost carbon paste/InGaZnO junctions
abstract: IGZO-based Schottky diodes have applications in high-speed electronics. However, these devices generally require noble metals to form a Schottky contact, which was one of the problems for their early commercialization. This study demonstrates the successful use of a semi-transparent carbon paste (CP) that is low-cost and which has a high work function as the Schottky contact for a Schottky junction for a-IGZO. The effect of the sintering temperature for CP on the resistivity, bulk crystallization, number of defects and work function (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\Phi$</tex>) are respectively determined by four-point resistivity measurement, X-ray diffraction, Raman spectroscopy, and surface Kelvin probe microscopy. The electrical properties of the Schottky diodes are also determined using current-voltage measurements and capacitance-voltage characteristics. After sintering, the crystalline quality of CP is improved so the series resistance of IGZO-based Schottky diodes decreases. Increasing the sintering temperature of the CP produces an increase in the work function of 0.18 eV, which gives a higher Schottky barrier height and better rectified performance. Using CP as the Schottky contact allows the manufacture of low-cost high performance IGZO-based Schottky diodes. It is hence expected that our scheme will be of great importance for the IGZO-based Schottky diode in the industrial application integrated with transistors.

articleTitle: Observation of a.c. Josephson effect in gate tunable Josephson junction on topological insulator (Bi0.2Sb0.8)2 Te3 films
abstract: In the past decade, Majorana Fermions (MFs) has been getting much interest because of their non-Abelian statistics and their application for topological quantum computation. One of the promising system hosting MFs is the hybrid structures between topological insulators (TIs) and s-wave superconductors. As the probe of MFs, measurements of a.c. Josephson effect, i.e. the Shapiro steps and Josephson radiation, is a useful tool. We fabricated Josephson junction on the 3D TI (Bi<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">0.2</inf>Sb<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">0.8</inf>)<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf>Te<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf> grown on SrTiO<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf>(111) substrate. We found that the supercurrent and the normal resistance of Josephson junction is gate-tunable and that the dominant carriers in the sample are from the topological surface states. Next, we measured the a.c. Josephson effects. In the Shapiro step measurement, we observed the both even and odd integer multiple of hf/2e steps. This contradicts with the existence of MFs in which odd multiple steps are expected to disappear. Furthermore, we also observed Josephson radiation with frequency of 2eV/h but no emission with frequency eV/h, a signature of MFs, is observed. We speculate that these results are due to huge dielectric constant of the substrate. Our experiment is the first report of a.c. Josephson effect on the gate-tunable Josephson junction of 3D TI film.

articleTitle: Effects of p-doping on excited spin states and the dynamics in InGaAs quantum dots
abstract: We study effects of p-doping on excited spin dynamics of InGaAs quantum dots (QDs) by circularly polarized time-resolved photoluminescence (PL). At excited states of p-doped QDs, the circular polarization degree (CPD) values are twice higher than those of undoped QDs. We attribute this enhanced CPD at excited states to spin-selective energy relaxation from the excited states to ground state. This can be promoted by the suppression of state filling at the ground state, which is induced by the decrease of PL lifetime due to the resident hole population.

articleTitle: Buried Tunnel Junction VCSEL with High Contrast Grating Top Reflector
abstract: Emerging applications of optical sensing in consumer products, such as facial recognition based on structured light and time of flight proximity sensing, create high volume demand for low-cost illumination sources in the infrared wavelength range. Vertical Cavity Surface Emitting Lasers (VCSELs), manufactured into arrays of tens to thousands of elements, show superior beam quality compared to LEDs and edge emitter lasers and sufficient power for most applications. In this paper we present a high contrast grating enabled VCSEL with a buried tunnel junction emitting in the 980 nm wavelength range. The presented architecture with lithographically defined current aperture promises potential for highly uniform and dense VCSEL arrays. In our work we describe an epitaxial regrowth process for VCSELs incorporating a GaAs tunnel junction. Prototype single emitter devices with aperture sizes from <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$6-12\ \mu \mathrm{m}$</tex> where fabricated. Devices with <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$6-8\ \mu \mathrm{m}$</tex> apertures achieved submilliamp thresholds, while devices with <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$12 \ \mu \mathrm{m}$</tex> apertures demonstrated 1.4 mW peak power and a thermal resistance of 1.21 K/mW.

articleTitle: Thermoelectrically Cooled nBn T2SLs InAs/InAsSb/B-AlAsSb MWIR Detector
abstract: The paper reports on the nBn barrier mid-wave infrared InAs/InAsSb (x<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">Sb</sub>=0.4) type-II superlattice detector operating in thermoelectrical cooling condition. AlAsSb (y<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">Sb</sub>=0.975) was proved to be proper material not introducing extra barriers in valence band in analysed temperature range in nBn architectures. Detectivity ~10<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">10</sup> cmHz<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">1/2</sup>/W at 200 K is reported without immersion lens.

articleTitle: Bio-sensing of small peptides by open sandwich immunoassay on graphene FETs
abstract: Graphene is suitable material for sensors because of high mobility and chemical stability. Recently graphene field effect transistors (FETs) have been applied for sensitive bio-sensors. In graphene FET bio-sensors, biomaterials are detected by changes of graphene electrical properties. However, Graphene FET biosensors cannot electrically detect targets which do not change electric characteristics of graphene. Here, we focused on open sandwich immunoassay which is antigen-antibody complex reaction by two antigen binding fragments (VH and VL). If VH are modified on graphene and detectable materials like ions were modified on VL, undetectable antigens can be detected. In this study, we have demonstrated sensitive detection of small peptides which is difficult to detect directly in graphene FETs and selectively detected using open sandwich immunoassay.

articleTitle: InP membrane lasers and active-passive integration
abstract: In this paper we review the recent developments in the nanophotonic platform IMOS. High-performance optical amplifier based on twin-guide active-passive integration scheme has been demonstrated, enabling continuous wave operated lasers on IMOS. Future work will seek to integrate more advanced components, such as detectors, polarization controllers and optical modulators in the same membrane.

articleTitle: Impact of Substrate Miscut Angle on Surface Morphology and Electrical Properties of Homoepitaxial $\pmb{\beta}$ -Ga2O3 Grown by MOVPE
abstract: The influence of substrate miscut on the surface morphology and Hall mobility at optimized growth conditions of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\beta$</tex>-Ga<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf>O<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf> layers was investigated. The results demonstrate that the surface morphology and the Hall mobility are impacted by the miscut angle of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\beta$</tex>-Ga<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf>O<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf> substrates. For substrates with miscut angle of 6° and a growth rate of about 4 nm/min, a morphology with step bunches was observed and a Hall mobility of the layer of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$115\pm 10$</tex> cm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup>/(Vs) was obtained. Using substrates with 4° miscut, step-flow growth mode and an enhancement of the Hall mobility about <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$135\pm 10\ \mathrm{cm}^{2}/(\mathrm{Vs})$</tex> was achieved.

articleTitle: $\beta$-Ga2O3 MOSFETs with Nitrogen-Ion-Implanted Back-Barrier: DC Performance and Trapping Effects
abstract: <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\beta$</tex>-Ga<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf>O<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf> has captured attention in recent years for power electronics. Opportunities also exist for <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\beta$</tex>-Ga<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf>O<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf> transistors to operate as radio-frequency amplifiers. For highly-scaled devices, strong confinement of the channel is critical for mitigating short-channel effects. In this work, a depletion-mode <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$n$</tex>-channel <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\beta$</tex>-Ga<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf>O<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf> MOSFET with a back-barrier formed by implantation of deep nitrogen acceptors was demonstrated. Despite being fabricated on a conductive base material, the device delivered a drain current density of 103 mA/mm commensurate with the channel charge density and a large output current on/off ratio of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$4\times 10^{9}$</tex>, both of which attested to the efficacy of back-barrier isolation. Pulsed current-voltage measurements revealed the presence of electron trapping under the gate manifested as a threshold voltage shift. The dominant charge trapping effect was mitigated instead of exacerbated by applying a large reverse gate bias - a behavior consistent with field-assisted trap emission. These results indicate a need for further process optimization to improve the speed and reliability of the device.

articleTitle: Spin dependent transport properties of spin bipolar transistors using a (Ga, Fe)Sb/(In, Fe)As p-n junction
abstract: Spin bipolar transistors (SBTs) with spin dependent output characteristics can be applied to non-volatile memory cells and reconfigurable logic circuits. III-V based carrier-induced ferromagnetic semiconductors (FMSs) are suitable materials for realizing SBTs, because they are compatible with non-magnetic III-V semiconductors with respect to the crystal structure and conductivity. In particular, Fe-based FMSs are promising materials for SBTs because both p-type and n-type FMSs are available and their ferromagnetism is maintained at room temperature. In this study, we fabricated spin bipolar transistors using a (Ga, Fe)Sb/(In, Fe)As p-n junction on top of a p-n-p AlGaAs/GaAs heterojunction bipolar transistor structure, grown by molecular beam epitaxy. We obtained the modulation of the collector current by the base voltage and the magnetoresistance (MR) effect. The bias dependence and temperature dependence of MR suggest that the observed MR signal is likely to originate from the spin-valve effect at the ferromagnetic (Ga, Fe)Sb/(In, Fe)As p-n junction. Our results indicate that Fe-based FMSs are promising for semiconductor spintronics devices.

articleTitle: Template-assisted selective epitaxy for III-V vertical nanowires on Si tandem solar cells
abstract: Solar cells incorporating III-V nanowires have attracted much attention recently to increase the window of spectral absorption of the current photovoltaic technology based on silicon. This work uses a novel template-assisted selective epitaxy (TASE) to grow III-V nanowires on Si by filling a pre-defined hollow SiO<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sub> template. We discuss the developed template fabrication steps and demonstrate the integration of GaAs and InGaP nanowires on Si with well-controlled shape, dimensions and composition. This work demonstrates a new step towards the realization of III-V/Si tandem solar cells.

articleTitle: Semi-ballistic thermal phonon transport in Sil-xGex nanowires
abstract: Length-dependent thermal conductivity in <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\text{Si}_{1-\mathrm{x}}\text{Ge}_{\mathrm{x}}$</tex> nanocrystalline nanowires was investigated. We found that phonon transport in <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\text{Si}_{1-\mathrm{x}}\text{Ge}_{x}$</tex> nanowires is in the intermediate regime between ballistic and diffusive transport. In addition, the ballisticity of phonons changes with temperature and Ge composition. As the temperature increases and Ge composition decreases, heat conduction becomes more diffusive, but remains semi-ballistic even at room temperature. This series of experiments supports previous theoretic works and provides us with further understanding of heat conduction in nanoscale.

articleTitle: Epitaxial Lift-Off of Ultrathin Heterostructures for Hot-Carrier Solar Cell Applications
abstract: Epitaxial lift-off, the separation of a device from its growth substrate through selective etching, is economically attractive for all III-V solar cells, enabling the reuse of the same substrate multiple times. It is even more interesting for ultrathin solar cells, where substrate removal is needed to implement light trapping. One promising example of ultrathin cells is the hot-carrier solar cell, a high-efficiency concept where the photo-generated electrons are at a higher temperature than the lattice. Our work focuses on these hot carriers, and the necessity for light trapping to develop high-efficiency hot-carrier solar cells. In this presentation, we report on the epitaxial lift-off of ultrathin GaAs-AlGaAs heterostructures. We bond these devices on gold, and separate them from their substrate using HCl to selectively etch an InAlP release layer. This method could be applied to all heterostructures that do not contain InP-based compounds. The photoluminescence spectrum is very similar before and after epitaxial lift-off, with a lower intensity we are working on improving. Our objective is to observe hot carriers in these devices. This would enable to study the influence of light trapping on hot carriers, and to implement these results into complete hot-carrier solar cells.

articleTitle: Effects of the Growth Environment on the Phase Stability of Sputter-deposited CdxZn1-xO Alloys
abstract: ZnO and CdO, having wurtzite (WZ) and rocksalt (RS) crystal structures, respectively, form alloys that have a structural phase transition window strongly dependent on deposition methods and conditions. WZ phase <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\text{Cd}_{\mathrm{x}}\text{Zn}_{1-\mathrm{x}}\mathrm{O}$</tex> alloys exhibit a direct bandgap that is largely tunable from 3.3 eV to 1.8 eV. However, at high Cd concentration phase separation tends to occur and achieving single-phase <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\text{Cd}_{\mathrm{x}}\text{Zn}_{1-\mathrm{x}}\mathrm{O}$</tex> alloys with <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\mathrm{x} > 0.4$</tex> is challenging. In this work, we present the materials properties of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\text{Cd}_{\mathrm{x}}\text{Zn}_{1-\mathrm{x}}\mathrm{O}$</tex> alloys synthesized using radio frequency magnetron sputtering and investigated the effects of deposition conditions on the phase transition behaviors. At a nominal growth temperature of 230°C a mixture of both WZ and RS phases were found in alloys for a wide composition window of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$0.4 < \mathrm{x} < 0.7$</tex>. With the addition of oxygen gases during sputter deposition, the WZ-to-RS phase transition composition was extended to <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\mathrm{x} > 0.6$</tex> and becomes much narrower. Density functional theory calculations show a lower formation energy for the wurtzite phase for alloys up to x∼0.75 with the presence of excess O in the form of O interstitials. These results present a convenient way to extend the composition of wurtzite-<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\text{Cd}_{\mathrm{x}}\text{Zn}_{1-\mathrm{x}}\mathrm{O}$</tex> alloys to bandgaps within the visible range for opto-electronic applications including photovoltaics.

articleTitle: Low temperature growth of h-BN on graphene via molecular beam epitaxy
abstract: Hexagonal boron nitride has emerged as a fundamental building block for atomically thin electronic devices. This contribution investigates its formation on graphene via molecular beam epitaxy at temperatures well below 1300°C, where it is considered metastable as a bulk material. However, it is shown that even at lower temperatures single- to few-layer hexagonal boron nitride still nucleates on graphene, and that the formation of the sp<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup>- and sp<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</sup>-bonded phases of BN can be manipulated via an in-situ N<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf>-plasma pretreatment of the substrates. Here the experimental discovery of a novel, metastable, sp<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</sup>-bonded phase, which so far has been only predicted theoretically, demonstrates a rich polymorphism in BN at the nanoscale.

articleTitle: Low 0.3 V Turn-on of Gated-Anode GaN-Cap/AlGaN/GaN HEMT Diode with Selective Dry-Etching Technique
abstract: We show low 0.3 V turn-on voltage diode characteristics using a gated-anode GaN-cap/AlGaN/GaN HEMT with highly threshold-voltage controllable technique with selective dry-etching of GaN over AlGaN. Also, equivalent circuit model extracted from S-parameter measurement results indicate an <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\mathrm{R}\times \mathrm{C}$</tex> component of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$250\ \mathrm{pF}\Omega$</tex>, i.e., a cut-off frequency of about 600 MHz.

articleTitle: Detection of Nonradiative Recombination Levels in UV-LEDs by Irradiating Below-Gap Excitation Light
abstract: It is important to connect photoluminescence (PL) characterization at low excitation condition with LED performance at higher carrier-density region. Nonradiative recombination (NRR) centers in a current-driven UV-LEDs were detected by EL intensity change and current increase when a below-gap excitation (BGE) light irradiates the LED. Based on a circuital consideration, the EL intensity change under constant-current condition and the current increase under constant-voltage condition are turned out to be effective indices of NRR centers. The latter increased with increasing the drive current up to 400 mA in addition to a close correspondence with the former at low density region. We consider that the current increase can be utilized to trace the contribution of NRR centers in a wider range of carrier density. The BGE energy dependence of the EL intensity change and current increase gives us a direct clue of NRR centers in UV-LEDs and can be utilized for materials and process optimization.

articleTitle: Dilute Waveguide Reflective Semiconductor Optical Amplifier for 3D Hybrid Silicon Photonics Integration
abstract: A dilute waveguide reflective semiconductor optical amplifier for alignment tolerant hybrid silicon photonics integration was demonstrated with emitting wavelength of 1.55 μm. Far field divergence angle at fast diverge axis was 11.8° compares to conventional waveguide of 28.2°. The dilute waveguide demonstrated 45% alignment tolerance improvement with mode size of 84 μm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup>.

articleTitle: Current injection and light confinement for UVB light emitting devices with graded p-AlGaN
abstract: An optimized graded p-AlGaN in which average AlN molar fraction is 0.55 was used for p-type layer in ultraviolet (UV)-B light emitting device. The maximum current density at 20 kA/cm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup> was achieved by optimizing graded p-AlGaN structure especially in the region at high AlN molar fraction. A single peak emission at 295 nm from MQW was obtained from the backside of sapphire substrate.

articleTitle: Effects of post-growth annealing in vacuum and Zn vapor on the electrical and optical properties of magnetron sputtered GaMgZnO films
abstract: The Ga<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">0.04</inf>Mg<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">0.10</inf>Zn<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">0.86</inf>O films with high transmittance have been magnetron sputtered in Ar or O<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf> plasma and post-growth annealed within vacuum and Zn vapor. It was observed that the optical band-gap and the film conductivity significantly increased after annealing in vacuum and Zn vapor. The resistivity and the optical bandgap of the ZnMgGaO film prepared in O<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf> plasma changed from <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$2\times 10^{2}\ \Omega \mathrm{cm}$</tex> and 3.34 eV to <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$1.3\times 10^{-3}\ \Omega \mathrm{cm}$</tex> and 3.60 eV after annealed in Zn vapor and those for the films grown in Ar plasma from <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$2\times 10^{-2}\ \Omega \mathrm{cm}$</tex> and 3.64 eV to <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$3.0\times 10^{-3}\ \Omega \mathrm{cm}$</tex> and 3.72 eV. Results of further detailed investigation including results of XPS and XRD and discussions on the defect behavior of the samples during the treatments will be discussed during the presentation.

articleTitle: InAs/GaAs Quantum Dot Intermixing by Dry Etching and Ion Implantation
abstract: In this paper, we applied the quantum dot intermixing (QDI) technique developed for 1550nm-band InAs QD to 1300nm-band InAs/GaAs QD. Two methods of defect introduction for QDI were employed such as ICP-RIE (Ar<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">+</sup>) and ion implantation (B+). As a result, about 80nm PL wavelength peak shift was obtained for ICP-RIE when annealing was performed at 575°C, after etching down to 450 nm to the QD layer. On the other hand, about 110nm wavelength shift was obtained for B+ implantation at an acceleration voltage of 120 keV and a dose of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$1.0\times 10^{14}/\mathbf{cm}^{2}$</tex> and subsequent annealing.

articleTitle: Molecular Beam Epitaxial Growth of InSb and AlSb Heterostructure on InSb Substrates
abstract: Surface morphology of epitaxial InSb and AISb layers grown on (001) InSb substrate is reported. The growth is done by molecular beam epitaxy. Attempt to realize planar crystalline InSb layer is made. Preliminary promising results are obtained with in-situ reflection high electron energy diffraction and atomic force microscopy observations.

articleTitle: Electrical and structural properties of Sn-doped $\alpha$-Ga2O3 thin films grown by mist chemical vapor deposition
abstract: We report on the structural and electrical properties of Sn-doped Ga<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf>O<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf> (GTO) thin films on c-sapphire substrates grown by mist chemical deposition (mist CVD). Gallium(III) acerylacetonate (Ga(acac)<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf>) and either Sn(acac)<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf> or tin(II) chloride dehydrate were used as source materials of Ga and Sn, respectively. Each solution of Ga (SGa) and Sn (SSn), which the source materials are solved in deionized water and a small amount of hydrochloric acid, was prepared at the concentration of 0.05 mol/L, and the solutions mixed with different ratio were used for the growth. With increasing the ratio of Sn solution (SSn/(SGa+SSn)), the concentration of Sn incorporated into the film was increased. The electrical conductivity was obtained in the films with the Sn concentration of less than 0.34 %. The crystal structure was maintained to <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\alpha$</tex>-Ga<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf>O<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf> in this Sn concentration range, while the crystal quality rapidly deteriorates when the concentration of Sn was over 0.34 %.

articleTitle: Irradiation Effects on Induced Electron Conductivity in an un-doped GaAs/AlGaAs Quantum Well Hall Bar
abstract: We measure conductivity and light response of a top gated electric field-induced 2DEG carrier in a GaAs based quantum-well heterostructure to confirm their stability as a consequence of removing the Si doping layer. Etched sidewall contacting techniques and surface treatment studies allowed carrier induction in a quantum-dot-fabrication compatible device structure. We performed quantum Hall measurements to evaluate the conduction stability and observed temporal decays of the induced carriers and illumination at several conditions that could still be redeemed by choosing proper fabrication techniques and operation voltage conditions. Mesoscopic research on such un-doped devices have possibility of efficiently interfacing single photons and single electron spins whereas that of holes.

articleTitle: Probing alloy formation using different excitonic species: The particular case of InGaN
abstract: Since the 1960s, alloys are grouped into two classes, featuring bound states in the bandgap (I - GaP:N, ZnTe:O, etc.) or additional, non-discrete, band states (II - SiGe, GaAsP, InGaAs, etc.). Therefore, one can observe either a rich and informative zoo of excitons bound to isoelectronic impurities (I), or the typical bandedge emission of a semiconductor that shifts and broadens with rising isoelectronic doping (II). Because no such strongly localized excitons are found in the photoluminescence (PL) spectra of the investigated bulk In(x)Ga(1-x)N epilayers (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$0\leq \mathrm{x}\leq 2.4\%$</tex>, 100 nm thick, growth on bulk GaN substrates), we suggest to utilize shallow impurities as a tool to study the distribution of isoelectronic centers. By micro-PL, we directly observe an entire hierarchy of bound excitons related to silicon-indium complexes as individual, energetically sharp emission lines appear (full width at half-maximum <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\approx 300\mu \text{eV}$</tex>). In order to exemplify our approach, we determine nanoscopic parameters of the InGaN alloy like the exciton diffusion length. We expect that our spectroscopic analysis represents a general pathway for studying mixed crystal alloys associated to class II, which approaches the high level of spectroscopic sophistication evidenced in literature for class I alloys.

articleTitle: Fabrication of $02.5 \ \mu\mathrm{m}$ T-Gate AlInGaN/AlN/GaN HEMTs by I-Line Optical Lithography
abstract: In this report, we demonstrate an optical lithography process to fabricate T-gate AlInGaN/AlN/GaN high electron mobility transistors (HEMTs) on Si substrates with gate length down to 0.25 μm. The gate foot is defined by backfilling and etching a SiNx layer with a 0.6 μm wide window. The backfilled SiNx layer serves not only as the spacer layer that results in a reduced gate foot, but also as a passivation layer for reducing surface trap states. The fabricated AIInGaN/AlN/GaN HEMTs exhibit I<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">DSS</sub> of 537 mA/mm, transconductance of 439 mS/mm, current gain cut-off frequency (f<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">T</sub>) of 58 GHz, and power gain cut-off frequency (f<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">max</sub>) of 73 GHz.

articleTitle: Multi-band valley-protected topological edge states in GaAs-based nanophononic crystals with complete phononic bandgaps
abstract: Multi-band valley-protected topological edge states is numerically demonstrated in GaAs-based phononic crystal (PnC) slabs. Two Dirac degeneracies at different frequencies are lifted by rotation of triangular holes in the unit cells breaking the mirror symmetry, and complete phononic bandgaps (PnBGs) are obtained near each frequency. The topological properties of both PnBGs depend on the rotating direction of the triangular holes, which allows the structures to have different valley vortex chirality. The vortex patterns of the valley states near PnBGs show the opposite rotating direction of the mechanical energy flux in different PnC slabs, which indicate different topological properties. At the boundary between the topologically different structures, the valley-protected edge states appear in each bandgap via the bulk-edge correspondence. The robust transports of the both valley-protected edge states are clearly observed in Z-shaped wave guides with the sharp corners of the boundary by numerical simulation. Our design paves the way toward multi-functional topological phononic devices with low energy loss through the multiple complete PnBGs.

articleTitle: Evaluation of Rabi frequency and coherence time in the hyperfine structure of 167Er3+ in Y2SiO5 through coherent transients
abstract: We demonstrate coherent transients -Rabi oscillation and a photon echo- between hyperfine levels in isotopically purified <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">167</sup>Er<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3+</sup> in Y<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf>SiO<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">5</inf> crystal at zero magnetic field. These observations provide us with optical param-eters such as the Rabi frequency and coherence time, which are indispensable for coherent manipulation of <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">167</sup>Er<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3+</sup> electronic states. The estimated coherence time is longer than that in degenerated levels, which indicates that the use of the hyperfine sublevels in <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">167</sup>Er<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3+</sup> is expected to exhibit longer memory time in quantum memories.

articleTitle: Direct Heteroepitaxy of Orientation-Patterned GaP on GaAs by Hydride Vapour Phase Epitaxy for Quasi-Phase-Matching Applications
abstract: Heteroepitaxial growth of orientation-patterned GaP on patterned GaAs template was developed by using hydride vapor phase epitaxy for quasi-phase-matching applications. We present the growth with well-defined periodic boundaries between (001) and (00 1) GaP domains. The GaP layer on planar GaAs was characterized by terahertz time-domain spectroscopy and the conductivity of GaP (0.16 S cm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">-1</sup>) was obtained in terahertz range.

articleTitle: Influence of post-annealing on properties of $\alpha$-Ga2O3 epilayer grown by halide vapor phase epitaxy
abstract: Effect of annealing to realize high-quality α-Ga<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sub>O<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</sub> epilayers grown by halide vapor phase epitaxy has been studied. The structural and optical properties of α-Ga<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sub>O<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</sub> changed with changing annealing duration. In particular, for an annealing duration of 3 min, the crystal quality improved from 51 and 2757 arcsec to 28 and 1539 arcsec for (0006) and (10-14) FWHM, respectively. X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy results confirmed that the oxygen gas during annealing reacted to compensate the oxygen vacancies in the α-Ga<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sub>O<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</sub> epilayers. These results show that the optimized thermal annealing improved the crystal quality of α-Ga<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sub>O<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</sub> epilayers.

articleTitle: Resonant-Cavity Infrared Detector (RCID) with Very Thin Absorber
abstract: A resonant-cavity detector incorporating only 5 quantum wells within the absorbing region has a peak sensitivity at 4.0 μm with a measured external quantum efficiency at room temperature of 34 % and dark current density comparable with state-of-the-art HgCdTe detectors.

articleTitle: Development of n-type GaN film by Si and Ti co-sputtering technique on a glass substrate
abstract: In this paper, the n-type GaN films were developed by using the Si and Ti co-sputtering technique and a ZnO buffer layer on amorphous glass substrates with different post-growth annealing temperatures for optimizing the GaN crystal quality. The GaN target was employed for the sputtering deposition of GaN films with the DC-Pulse sputtering power of 75W, while the Si and Ti targets were adopted as the doping species with the RF sputtering power of 30W, and the DC-sputtering power of 20W, respectively. The GaN films with the thermal annealing temperature of 400 oC revealed the low thin-film resistivity of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$2.6\times 10^{-1}$</tex> ohm-cm for the Si-Ti co-doped n-type GaN film with a high electron concentration of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$6.65\times 10^{19}$</tex> cm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">−3</sup> using the Hall measurement. The XRD results revealed a high (002) XRD intensity with a narrow spectral line FWHM value which indicated the superior crystal growth of hexagonal structure for the GaN thin films. In addition, the PL measurement results presented the near band edge emission at 365 nm which indicated the crystal growth of the GaN thin films on glass substrates.

articleTitle: Using optical emission spectroscopy (OES) to monitor In-line very high-frequency plasma enhanced chemical vapor deposition (VHF-PECVD) technique optoelectrical properties
abstract: In this paper using optical emission spectroscopy (OES) to monitor In-line very high-frequency plasma enhanced chemical vapor deposition (VHF-PECVD) technique optoelectrical properties. In-line VHF-PECVD was developed by MIRDC (Metal Industries Research & Development Centre) in Taiwan. In-line VHF-PECVD system with an electrode distance was 15 to 50 mm and electrode area of 1681 cm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup>. Due to the difference between the observation port and the plasma position. Therefore, this paper developed an online VHF-PECVD internal optical system to verify the stability of the internal optical system. The OES is a non-intrusive monitoring device that is widely used for real-time monitoring and stabilization devices for plasma monitoring. This paper used OES to monitor the stability of processed silicon thin films.

articleTitle: Long-term stability of organic physically unclonable function for IoE security
abstract: We evaluated long-term stability of organic security circuit for future IoE society. Physically unclonable function (PUF) was chosen as basic technology in this study, because PUF utilized dynamic information such as characteristics variation in devices and it was expected to show high tamper resistance. In addition, we utilized organic semiconductor because of its advantage for flexibility. At first, we fabricated organic thin film transistor array to measure current variation. Comparing current in on-state of organic transistor, we obtained 19-bit unique number depending on a chip. During measurement for 6 months, on-current gradually decreased as time goes by. However, the unique number was generated stably with low bit error rate below 11% when we set benchmark to data at 7th day after fabrication. It means the unique number can be handled as device ID. It is because organic transistors degraded uniformly over all. As a result, our organic transistor array works well as PUF even after 174 days.

articleTitle: Improved Electrical Degradation of AlInGaN/GaN HEMT by using Triethylgallium Grown GaN channel and Cap
abstract: A comparison of electrical degradation of AlInN and AlInGaN HEMT with their GaN channel grown by trimethylgallium (TMG)/ triethylgallium (TEG) has been studied in details. A notable reduction in dynamic Ron and current collapse is observed by growing the GaN channel with TEG precursor. AlInN HEMT with TEG grown GaN channel exhibits lower dynamic Ron, current collapse and transconductance dispersion as opposed to TMG grown GaN channel. We attribute this improved device performance due to more than one order of magnitude reduction in residual carbon in the TEG grown GaN channel. Pulsed transconductance and I<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">d</inf>-V<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">g</inf> measurements indicate acceptor like trap states under the gate and gate-drain access region. Further improvement in device degradation is also observed by replacing the AlInN barrier with the AlInGaN barrier, having the same TEG grown GaN channel. Therefore, the AlInGaN barrier seems to be more immune to charge trapping than that of AlInN barrier.

articleTitle: Photonic-crystal Lasers with Extremely Short Embedded Active-regions
abstract: We have fabricated an InP-based lambda-scale embedded active-region photonic-crystal (LEAP) laser with an extremely short active-region length of just the lattice constant (∼430 nm) of the photonic crystal (PhC). We have achieved lasing with a low threshold current of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$8.7\ \mu \mathrm{A}$</tex> at room temperature. Still, this threshold is rather high compared with those with two (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$4.9\ \mu \mathrm{A}$</tex>) or three times (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$6.6\ \mu \mathrm{A}$</tex>) longer active regions. The dependence of the static characteristics on the active-region length is discussed, which infers that improvement in the current injection structure is necessary for further reduction in the operation energy of LEAP lasers with such extremely short active regions.

articleTitle: Demonstration of Low-Resistive P-Type Cu4O3 Thin Films by Radio Frequency Sputtering for Low-Cost Thin Film Solar Cells
abstract: A systematic investigation on the influence of oxygen flow rates and substrate positions on the structural, optical and electrical properties of copper oxide (Cu<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">x</inf>O) thin films deposited by reactive radio frequency sputtering to establish the deposition condition for Cu<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">4</inf>O<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf>. Detailed analyses on x-ray diffraction (XRD) and Raman spectroscopy were performed, revealing that different single or bi-phase of Cu<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf>O, Cu<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">4</inf>O<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf> and CuO were grown at the different O<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf> flow rate and substrate position. From the optical absorption analyses, Cu<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf>O films showed a direct forbidden transition at <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{g}}=2.28\sim 2.37\ \text{eV}$</tex> in addition to a direct allowed transition at <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{g}}=2.50\sim 2.53\ \text{eV}$</tex>. In Cu<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">4</inf>O<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf> and CuO films, a direct forbidden transition at <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{g}}=1.58\ \text{eV}$</tex> and 1.51 ∼ 1.54 eV was observed respectively with a high absorption coefficient, demonstrating the possibility to use these compounds as an absorber for single junction solar cells. Moreover, single phase Cu<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">4</inf>O<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf> showed the resistivity from 38 to 460 ohm cm with p-type conductivity, which was the lowest resistivity for the single phase of Cu<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">4</inf>O<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf> films reported so far.

articleTitle: Magnetic anisotropy switching in heavily-Fe-doped high-Curie-temperature ferromagnetic semiconductor (Ga0.7, Fe0.3)Sb with a critical thickness
abstract: Ferromagnetic semiconductor (FMSs), which exhibits both magnetic and semiconducting properties, are promising for semiconductor-based spintronics devices. Magnetic anisotropy (MA) plays an important role in determining the magnetization direction of ferromagnetic materials. Here, we present the thickness-dependence control of MA in (Ga<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">0.7</inf>, Fe<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">0.3</inf>)Sb by growing samples with different thicknesses <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$d=20-55\ \text{nm}$</tex> grown on AlSb by low-temperature molecular beam epitaxy. We used ferromagnetic resonance (FMR) to estimate the MA constants of the (Ga<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">0.7</inf>, Fe<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">0.3</inf>)Sb. We systematically measured the dependence of the FMR resonance field on the external magnetic-field direction and fitted a theoretical curve to obtain the MA fields of the (Ga, Fe)Sb thin films, and obtained the effective MA constants (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$K_{\text{eff}}$</tex>) of (Ga, Fe)Sb. From the sign of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$K_{\text{eff}}$</tex>, we found that MA changes from in-plane magnetic anisotropy (IMA) to perpendicular magnetic anisotropy (PMA) with increasing <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$d$</tex>. To understand this, we separated the <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$K_{\text{eff}}$</tex> into the volume contribution (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$K_{\mathrm{V}}$</tex>) and the interface contribution (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$K_{\mathrm{I}}$</tex>). We show that the IMA originates from the film interface due to the tensile strain when the films are thin, whereas <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$K_{\mathrm{V}}$</tex> causes PMA in (Ga, Fe)Sb. The observation of FMR at room temperature and control of MA are important steps towards device applications of (Ga, Fe)Sb.

articleTitle: Atmospheric Pressure Solution Growth of Monoisotopic Hexagonal Boron Nitride
abstract: Hexagonal boron nitride crystals with a single boron isotope (monoisotopic) were produced at atmospheric pressure from a molten metal solution of nickel and chromium. Crystals with both pure <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">10</sup>B and <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">11</sup>B were produced. Narrow Raman peaks widths of 3 cm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">-1</sup> and photoluminescence peaks at 5.75 eV demonstrate the crystals are high quality. The room temperature thermal conductivity of monoisotopic hBN is 40% higher than hBN with the natural distribution of boron, due to a lack of isotopic disorder. Because its phonon lifetimes are more than three times longer that natural hBN, monoisotopic hBN is a better for nanophotonics.

articleTitle: Structural and optical properties of GaAs film grown on a glass substrate using a large-grained Ge seed layer for solar cell applications
abstract: We fabricate a light absorbing GaAs layer on a glass substrate using a Ge seed layer formed by Al-induced crystallization. The GaAs layer grown at 520 °C exhibits the grain size of 50 μm and the internal quantum efficiency of 60% with a bias voltage of 1.0 V. These values are the largest among the GaAs layers grown on amorphous substrates at low temperatures (<; 600 °C).

articleTitle: Universal nuclear focusing of confined electron spins
abstract: For spin-based quantum computation in semiconductors, single electrons are confined in a volume that contains typically more than 10000 lattice atoms. Hyperfine interaction to the fluctuating nuclear spins of those atoms dephases the electron spin. It has been shown that dynamical decoupling techniques or a control of the nuclear background polarization can mitigate such dephasing. Here we investigate a method first discovered in self-assembled InAs quantum dots, where the nuclear background polarization can be focused to precise values by exposing the electron spins to periodical laser pulses. Thereby the electron-spin precession frequencies take on values at integer multiples of the laser repetition rate, leading to so-called spin mode-locking. Different explanations of such mode-locking have been proposed. We show that the effect is a universal phenomenon that also occurs in lithographically-defined many-electron GaAs/AlGaAs dots. We find that nuclear focusing is mediated by an optical Stark shift induced by the laser pulses and can be controlled by the laser wavelength. This opens the door to achieve long electron spin coherence times also in systems of confined electrons that can be controlled in shape, size and position.

articleTitle: Growth of Ga2(O,S)3 Alloy Films on YSZ Substrates by Mist Chemical Vapor Deposition
abstract: We fabricated Ga<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf>(O,S)<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf> films, alloys of Ga<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf>O<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf> with Ga<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf>S<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf>, on YSZ substrates by mist-CVD method. It is practically impossible to realize the p-type conductivity in Ga<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf>O<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf> films, because of the deep acceptor levels resulted from the deep valence energy position. We are trying to conquer the problem by alloying Ga<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf>O<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf> with Ga<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf>S<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf>, because Ga<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf>S<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf> exhibits p-type conductivity due to the energetically shallower valence band and acceptors. All the fabricated Ga<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf>(O,S)<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf> films were amorphous. Sulfur composition of Ga<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf>(O,S)<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf> films were successfully controlled at almost entire range by changing molar concentration of sulfur precursor in source. The surface morphology is largely varied with incorporation of sulfur atoms, suggesting the different growth modes of Ga<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf>(O,S)<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf> films.

articleTitle: The thermal stability of $\varepsilon$-Ga2O3 thin films grown on (111) 3C-SiC template substrates
abstract: The thermal stability of ε-Ga<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sub>O<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</sub> thin films grown on a (111) 3C-SiC template was investigated by X-ray diffraction. C-axis-aligned single-phase ε-Ga<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sub>O<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</sub> thin films grown at 350 °C by mist chemical vapor deposition were annealed from 700 to 900 °C in air ambient. The structure of the as-grown ε-Ga<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sub>O<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</sub> thin films changed from pure single-phase ε-Ga<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sub>O<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</sub> to a mixed-phase with ε-Ga<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sub>O<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</sub> and β-Ga<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sub>O<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</sub> after annealing at 850 °C. Furthermore, 900 °C annealing made it completely transit to β-Ga<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sub>O<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</sub>. These results indicated that the thermal stability of the mist-CVD grown ε-Ga<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sub>O<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</sub> films is comparable to that of previously reported films grown by other methods. This critical temperature will limit the process temperature for device fabrication, especially for the active region formation by the ion implantation process in order to make satisfactory ohmic contact.

articleTitle: Spin-conserved electron transport to InGaAs quantum dots through GaAs/AlGaAs superlattice
abstract: We report on the spin-conserved electron transport to self-assembled InGaAs quantum dots (QDs) through GaAs/AlGaAs superlattice (SL) by circularly polarized time-resolved photoluminescence spectroscopy of the QD excited states with the selective excitation for the SL minibands. The spin transport properties largely depend on the AlGaAs barrier thickness of the SL. The SL with a thinner barrier demonstrates a quantum spin transport to QDs with highly conserving the electron-spin polarization during the transport process through the SL minibands.

articleTitle: Development of Carrier Concentration and Its Effects on the Electrical Stability of Al-doped ZnO Transparent Electrode in Harsh Environment
abstract: Transparent electrodes are widely applied in optoelectronic devices such as flat panel displays, photovoltaics, lightings, thin film transistors, etc. As the long-term usage of the devices is very important, the transparent electrodes should have good electrical stability. Al-doped ZnO (AZO) transparent electrode has been considered as the best replacement of the mostly used transparent electrode, Sn-doped In<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf>O<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf> (ITO), however, the electrical stability of AZO thin films is yet to be satisfactory. To improve it, this research investigated the influence of carrier concentration on the electrical stability. AZO thin films were prepared on glass substrates by RF magnetron sputtering at 100W of RF power with deposition duration of 60 minutes with a Zn metal target and 3 Al chips. Argon and oxygen gases were applied both at 30 sccm. Then thin films were annealed for 30 minutes in a hydrogen atmosphere at 400 to 550°C. After damp heat test with 85% of relative humidity at 85°C for 30 days, higher-temperature-annealed AZO thin films obtained better stability. Decrease of carrier concentration was more influential to the electrical stability than the decrease of mobility. Top oxide layer, which seemed to be spontaneously formed at higher temperature was effective to keep the carrier concentration.

articleTitle: Improvement of channel mobility and reliability in GaN-MOSFETs
abstract: The channel mobility and positive bias temperature instability is improved by the additional two processes of the gate structures in recessed normally-off GaN-MOSFETs. The one is the surface treatment for removal of the damage by the recess etching. The other is annealing process of gate insulator to reduce the impurity density drastically. These additional processes realize the channel mobility and reliability improvement by the suppression of coulomb scattering and the trap reduction at the gate insulators.

articleTitle: Visualization of Carrier Transport in Organic-Inorganic Perovskite Field-Effect Transistor by Electric-Field-Induced Optical Second-Harmonic Generation (EFISHG)
abstract: Carrier motion in the perovskite thin films is directly visualized by the time-resolved EFISHG technique. Appropriate laser wavelength near the band edge enabled us to observe the electric field in the perovskite layer selectively. Carrier mobility has been estimated by analyzing the transient carrier motion as 0.02 cm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup>/Vs. EFISHG technique provides an effective way for studying the carrier motions in organic-inorganic perovskite thin film.

articleTitle: Two-dimensional photonic crystal phosphors for efficient and polarization-insensitive excitation
abstract: As a continuing effort to improve the performance of photonic crystal (PhC) phosphors—an engineered nanophotonic phosphor structure developed by the authors' group—we hereby introduce two-dimensional (2D) PhC phosphor films. In particular, the excitation polarization dependence inherent to and suffered by the precedent one-dimensional PhC phosphors can be eliminated using a square lattice PhC structure due to its four-fold rotational symmetry. In addition, the thickness of the high index PhC backbone layer is intentionally increased so that dual excitation resonances occur for both the transverse-electric (TE) and transverse-magnetic (TM) waveguide modes, thereby effectively doubling the phosphor efficiency. We implemented and examined 2D PhC phosphor structures with colloidal quantum dots (CQDs) as phosphor material. We observed ∼4 times enhanced and excitation-polarization-insensitive CQD fluorescence at dual resonance wavelengths for the TE- and TM-guided modes. We confirmed the validity of the observed results through simulations.

articleTitle: Selective area epitaxy of GaP nanowire array on Si (111) by MOCVD
abstract: Because of its indirect bandgap nature, Gallium phosphide (GaP) in its conventional zinc blende crystal structure, has only limited optoelectronic applications in the visible light spectrum. The WZ structured GaP, on the other hand, has a direct band gap between 2.18 and 2.25 eV, ideal for a green-yellow spectral range light emitting devices. It is well known that the crystal structure of the III-V materials can be modulated when they are grown in nanowire (NW) form via the VLS/SAE mechanism so that either a ZB, WZ, or an intermixing of the ZB and WZ structured III-V NWs can be achieved. The realization of WZ GaP NWs were experimentally verified but the mechanism of selecting a crystal structure while NW is grown are still controversial. However, a common factor that promotes the realization of WZ structured NW is the suppression of the lateral overgrowth, because the ZB structure has the lowest surface energy at {11<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">-</sup>0} side facets of the hexagonal NW. On the other hand, the nucleation at side {11<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">-</sup>00} facets of WZ NW is difficult so that the hexagonal WZ NWs tend to grow more vertically with less lateral overgrowth. Understanding, developing, and controlling the growth condition of GaP NWs to form WZ structures would be crucial to practical applications of this highly promising material system. In addition, integrating GaP on silicon is also challenging. Recently, GaP nanowire (NW) heteroepitaxial growth have been demonstrated on Si (111) and Si (100) substrates using the VLS method. However, selective area epitaxy (SAE) of GaP NWs on Si (111) substrate or even on the GaP (111) substrate have not been well developed yet.

articleTitle: High Frequency Characteristics of AlInGaN HEMTs on Low Resistance Silicon for Millimeter-Wave Applications
abstract: This work demonstrates a high performance AlInGaN/AlN/GaN high electron mobility transistor grown on 150 mm p-type low resistance (resistivity ~20–100 ohm.cm) silicon substrate. Devices of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\mathrm{Lgs}/\mathrm{Lg}/\mathrm{Lgd}= 1/0.16/2\ \mathrm{um}$</tex> and <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\mathrm{Lgs}/\mathrm{Lg}/\mathrm{Lgd}= 1/0.16/4\ \mathrm{um}$</tex>, show similar DC characteristics with IDSS of 893 mA/mm and 854 mA/mm, transconductance of 370 mS/mm and 375 mS/mm, Ron of 0.175 mohm-cm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup> and 0.259 rnohm-cm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup>, and three terminal off-state breakdown (BV) voltage of 69 V and 127 V respectively. Current gain cut-off frequency (fT) of 83 GHz and 63 GHz and power gain cut-off frequency (fmax) of 95 GHz and 77 GHz with a high Johnson's figure-of-merits (J-FOM) of 5.7 THz-V and 8.0 THz-V are achieved on the devices with gate to drain distance of 2 um and 4 um respectively. After de-embedding the substrate effect, the fmax of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\mathrm{Lgd}\ =2\ \mathrm{um}$</tex> device increases from 95 GHz to only 105 GHz, indicating the influence of substrate is limited in the epilayer structure used in this work.
